bivy.name: Buttress bivy at the heather-to-rock transition
bivy.capacity: Small ledges and heather platforms; enough for a party of two, not a tent camp
bivy.water: Running water or snowmelt seeps are usually available here through summer; it dries out in a hot, low-snow year, so carry the capacity to melt or to go dry
bivy.permit: Overnight camping anywhere in the park backcountry needs a National Park Service permit; the peak falls in the Johannesburg cross-country zone, capped at six people per party and six parties per night
bivy.notes: This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, and it is what makes the route a two-day climb for most parties — it typically takes eight to twelve hours of climbing from the base of the buttress to reach it, with two to three hours of glacier and summit snow above. It sits where the steep heather and rock give way to the snow and glacier, so it is the last flat, watered ground before the upper mountain. It is also the point of no easy return: the ground below is 4,000 ft of steep brush, heather and rock above the valley, and retreating down it in the dark is far worse than sitting out the night. Wind is the main comfort variable; some nights are dead calm and warm, some are not.

bivy.name: Chopped platforms on the upper glacier
bivy.capacity: Whatever you cut — one or two bodies
bivy.notes: An improvised, secondary option above the standard bivy for parties who ran out of daylight higher up. Summer sun cupping means real work with an axe to get a flat platform, and it is fully exposed to wind and to crevasse hazard, so probe and anchor. Treat this as an emergency bivy rather than a plan.

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.capacity: Hardened sites in a zone capped at six parties per night, twelve people per party
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks and the permanent snowfield at the back of the basin; reliable all season, though the surface streams shrink late
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required, and Boston Basin is one of the few zones that accepts advance reservations rather than walk-up only. Composting toilets serve both the upper and lower camp areas.
bivy.notes: A comfortable planned camp, roughly 6,300 to 6,400 ft, on a small sandy flat at the foot of a permanent snowfield with a privy and a food storage bin nearby. This is the standard staging camp for the traverse: about two to two and a half hours from here to the base of Torment. It is the most crowded alpine camp in this part of the range, biting flies are notorious in midsummer, and the park rules that apply everywhere apply here — camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadows, and stay 100 ft back from water.

bivy.name: Torment Basin camp below the southeast face
bivy.capacity: Room for a small party; the zone allows six parties per night, twelve per party
bivy.water: Snowmelt from the surrounding snowfields and the Taboo Glacier; early in the season you may be chopping a platform out of snow rather than looking for water
bivy.permit: Separate cross-country zone from Boston Basin, so a party crossing the Torment saddle to sleep here needs Torment Basin on the permit itinerary
bivy.notes: A planned alternative camp for parties who want to start the traverse from the base of the climbing instead of from Boston Basin. It sits under the southeast side of Torment near the foot of the east couloir. Early in the season the ground is still part snow and gets excavated with an axe; late in the season the rocky patches are bare. It puts you above the basin traverse, which is the section that is genuinely easy to lose in a whiteout.

bivy.name: Mid-traverse ridge bivy
bivy.capacity: Two, on a flat notch — this is a ledge, not a campsite
bivy.water: A snowfield beside the notch, with running water audible under the boulders in some years; unreliable, and dry by late July or August in a low-snow year
bivy.notes: This is the emergency-and-committed option rather than a planned camp: a flat spot at a notch on the ridge roughly midway along the traverse, reached after the snow and ice section on the north side. Parties who get benighted mid-ridge use it, and parties intentionally splitting the traverse into two short days sleep there for the position — views out to Eldorado on one side and the Ptarmigan Traverse peaks on the other. Assume you may have to melt snow, and assume wind: there is no shelter on the crest.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites on bare ground in the rocky meadows plus a two-person bivy platform; the zone allows six parties a night, six people per party
bivy.water: Running streams through the basin fed by the snowfields above, reliable through the season but heavy with glacial silt — filter and treat it
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone. It is not one of the zones that takes advance reservations, so the permit is picked up in person.
bivy.notes: This is the standard base camp for the whole Southern Pickets and a genuinely comfortable one — a small flat gravelly basin with flowers, running water and a full view of the range, sitting about 400 ft below the notch in the ridge above it. It is a planned camp, not a bivy: parties sleep here, climb the peak, and come back to it. Getting to it is the hard part, roughly 7 miles and 5,700 ft of gain with a steep, chossy 400 ft descent off the notch to finish, so plan on arriving late and staying two nights rather than trying to move camp. Park rules bite here because the ground is meadow: pitch on gravel, rock or snow, never on vegetation, and stay 100 ft from the streams. There is no water at all on the last 3,500 ft of the approach, so fill up low.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.capacity: Multiple tent sites on bare ground in the rocky meadows, plus a bivy platform sized for two side by side with gear; the zone is capped at six parties per night and six people per party
bivy.water: Streams running through the basin flats from the snowfields above; dependable but silty, so filter and treat
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone; it is a walk-up zone rather than one of the reservable ones
bivy.notes: The planned camp for this route and effectively the only one — a flat gravelly basin roughly 400 ft below and north of the 6,200 to 6,350 ft notch that the approach crosses. Comfortable ground, water at hand, and a direct view of the Pickets. From here it is a long traverse over benches and slabs to the Terror Glacier and the gully to the col, so most parties treat it as a two-night camp and climb from it rather than moving up. The descent off the notch into the basin is the crux of getting here: loose and steep late season, a firm snow finger with a short steep headwall early. Camp on gravel or rock, not the heather, and keep 100 ft back from the water.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows
bivy.capacity: An established camp area with individual sites plus a group site; numbers are held down by a quota rather than by ground
bivy.water: Streams through the meadows, running all season; this is the last easy water before the glacier
bivy.permit: An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required and Glacier Meadows is quota'd — reservations are needed for the summer season and go on sale in advance through the federal recreation booking site. A bear canister is required beyond this point, and blue bags are mandatory on the mountain.
bivy.notes: The standard base camp at roughly 17 miles in, shaded and comfortable, with shelters, a bear wire and two working privies — the last toilets before the glacier. It sits about 4,175 to 4,300 ft depending on which part of the meadow you are in. From here the climbers' path runs about 0.8 mile up onto the lateral moraine crest and down onto the Blue Glacier. Camping is explicitly not allowed anywhere between Glacier Meadows and the glacier, so if the day runs long this is where you come back to. About a quarter mile before camp the trail crosses a washout on a roughly 100 ft ladder with a fixed rope, which is the hardest part of the walk in for most parties.

bivy.name: Snow Dome
bivy.capacity: Tent sites in the rocks of the lower dome and flatter ground on top near the weather station
bivy.permit: One of only two camp areas permitted above Glacier Meadows on this route; blue bags are required for all human waste here, and a bear canister is required beyond Glacier Meadows
bivy.notes: A high camp rather than an emergency bivy, and the reason parties use it is that it removes the glacier's lower miles from summit day. Reaching it means roped crevasse travel from the glacier toe, so it is not a place you retreat to casually in poor visibility. It is fully exposed on a broad snow dome — wind and weather with nothing to hide behind — and everything you drink has to be melted. The other permitted camp area up here is Caltech Rocks. Nothing between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier may be camped on.

bivy.name: Elk Lake
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, and Elk Lake is quota'd like Glacier Meadows, so the site has to be reserved
bivy.notes: About 15 miles in, where the Hoh River Trail stops being flat and starts climbing. It is the standard place to break the approach for parties who cannot make Glacier Meadows in a day, and the fallback if the snow slopes above it turn out to need axe and crampons, which they often do in early season. Sheltered forest camp, no alpine exposure — this is a comfort camp, not a mountain bivy.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass
bivy.capacity: One party per night, maximum six people — the tightest camp quota in the park's cross-country system
bivy.water: Snowmelt at the pass; running water in the gully below it early in the season, drying back as the season goes on, so late-season parties should expect to melt snow
bivy.permit: The Perfect Pass cross-country zone allows exactly one party of up to six per night on a National Park Service backcountry permit, and it is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one. If it is taken, there is no second site here.
bivy.notes: The planned high camp for this route and the one everything else is scheduled around. Ground is limited: early in the season much of the pass is still snow-covered and parties either camp on the snow or scout the sandy patches slightly higher on the ridge. It is a pass, so it is windy and weather-exposed with no shelter. Getting from camp onto the glacier is itself part of the climb — depending on melt-out it can mean around 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, so leaving camp in the dark or returning to it late is a real commitment, not a stroll.

bivy.name: Whatcom Pass camp
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp with a fixed number of sites assigned on the permit
bivy.water: Snowmelt and creeks at the pass
bivy.permit: A designated National Park Service backcountry camp; you may only camp in the camp area named on your permit itinerary for the date on it
bivy.notes: The last established camp before the committing ground, used by parties coming in on the Chilliwack River approach. From here you still have to get around Whatcom Peak to reach Perfect Pass — the direct north ridge is loose and very exposed and is not the way most parties go, while the standard workaround crosses the Whatcom Glacier on the peak's east side, which has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years. Treat this as the last comfortable night rather than a high camp.

bivy.name: Copper Creek camp
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp on the Chilliwack River Trail
bivy.permit: Designated National Park Service backcountry camp; permit itinerary must name it
bivy.notes: About 7.5 miles in on the valley approach, with reliable water and a pit toilet. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it exists on this list because the approach to Challenger is long enough that most parties sleep low at least once in each direction. It is also the sensible retreat target if the Chilliwack ford turns you around — the log crossings there are unreliable and have caught parties out.

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.capacity: Hardened sites; the zone allows six parties per night and up to twelve people per party
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks and the permanent snowfield behind camp, reliable through the season
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required. Boston Basin is one of the small number of zones that accepts advance reservations, and composting toilets serve both the upper and lower camp areas.
bivy.notes: The comfortable planned camp, roughly 6,300 to 6,400 ft on a sandy flat below a permanent snowfield, about three to four hours from the road. Everything on this route beyond it is committing, because the way onto the Boston Glacier goes over Sharkfin Col and that involves a rappel or a steep downclimb on poor rock that many parties describe as harder than the face itself. Coming back to this camp means reversing it. A lower camp at about 5,300 ft with its own composting toilet is the alternative if the upper sites are full.

bivy.name: Boston Glacier bivy
bivy.capacity: Whatever platform you cut; the Boston Glacier cross-country zone allows six parties per night, six people per party
bivy.permit: The glacier is its own cross-country zone on the park permit system, capped at six people per party and six parties per night; human waste on snow and glacier terrain has to be packed out in a blue bag
bivy.notes: A planned but fully exposed glacier bivy used to shorten summit day, on one of the largest glaciers in the lower 48. You are camping on a crevassed surface, so probe the platform and its surroundings before dropping the rope, and mark the perimeter. There is no shelter, no running water and no ground: everything is melted, and wind or a change in weather has nowhere to be dodged. The serious point is that it sits past Sharkfin Col — retreat from here means reclimbing that col, so committing to this bivy commits you to the route in a way that camping in Boston Basin does not.

bivy.name: Sahale–Boston col bivy
bivy.capacity: One small two-person tent's worth of flat ground
bivy.notes: A tiny, spectacular perch on the col between Sahale and Boston, used by parties linking this face with other climbs in the basin or descending over Sahale Arm. It is an emergency-sized site, not a camp: there is room for one small tent, and cornices overhang the Davenport side, so probe out from the sleeping platform before settling in and do not wander in the dark. Wind exposure is total.

bivy.name: Luna Col (Luna Pass)
bivy.capacity: A handful of bivy-sized spots on slabs and gravel; the Luna cross-country zone allows six parties a night, six people per party
bivy.water: A small snowfield sitting right at the saddle normally gives running water; by late season it is down to a shallow snowmelt pool, and in a hot low-snow year it may be gone entirely
bivy.permit: Camping needs a National Park Service backcountry permit; the col lies in the Luna cross-country zone, capped at six people per party and six parties per night
bivy.notes: The standard high camp and the base for summit day on Fury, reached after a long steep heather-and-talus traverse from Access Col. It is a planned camp but a rough one — glacially polished slabs with very few genuinely flat tent spots, so most parties bivy rather than pitch. Being a saddle it is fully wind-exposed with no shelter in any direction, and the water depends entirely on a snow patch that shrinks all summer, so check it rather than assume it. From here the summit involves several miles of ridge, a steep heather chute and a crevassed glacier, and this is the only sheltered ground you will come back to.

bivy.name: Access Basin camp
bivy.capacity: Open talus and brush ground with room for a small party; a flat-topped boulder is a known sleeping spot
bivy.water: Access Creek runs through the basin, and there is meltwater below the snowfields above it; reliable through the season
bivy.permit: Overnight camping requires a National Park Service backcountry permit
bivy.notes: A planned camp used to break the approach, at the head of Access Creek where the bushwhack finally opens onto talus. It is the last water before the long, hot, shadeless scree chute up to Access Col, and it is where most parties stash anything not needed above. It is not scenic or comfortable — brush, deadfall and biting insects — but it is flat, watered and low, which is the whole point after roughly 1,900 ft of devil's club and huckleberry. Coming down off the mountain, this is the target that turns an epic back into a walk out.
